props.title: The Manhattan Project
props.initialSlug: Teen builds atomic bomb to impress brilliant girl

sections.content: The Manhattan Project stands as a fascinating teen thriller that cleverly subverts both coming-of-age and Cold War narratives. Like WarGames (1983), it taps into Reagan-era nuclear anxieties through the lens of brilliant but reckless youth. Director Marshall Brickman, Woody Allen's former writing partner, brings unexpected wit to this story of a teenage genius who builds an atomic bomb to expose government secrets. The film sits at an intriguing intersection with other 80s tech-paranoia films like Real Genius (1985) and Short Circuit (1986), all exploring the moral implications of scientific advancement through young protagonists.

sections.content: Christopher Collet delivers a compelling performance as Paul Stephens, a science prodigy who steals plutonium from a government facility disguised as a medical research lab. His relationship with John Lithgow's Dr. Mathewson creates fascinating tension, as both characters represent different sides of scientific responsibility. This dynamic echoes through later films like Good Will Hunting (1997) and October Sky (1999), where brilliant young minds grapple with mentorship and moral obligations.

The film's treatment of nuclear technology feels especially relevant when viewed alongside other nuclear-themed films of the era like The Day After (1983) and Testament (1983). While those films dealt with apocalyptic scenarios, The Manhattan Project takes a more personal approach, using the bomb as a metaphor for knowledge and responsibility. This approach influenced later tech-thriller films like Sneakers (1992) and Hackers (1995). SUBHEAD: Cold War Science on Screen

sections.content: The film's portrayal of government scientific facilities reflects a specific moment in Cold War cinema, when the lines between civilian and military research became increasingly blurred. This theme appears in contemporaneous films like Project X (1987) and Weird Science (1985), but The Manhattan Project stands out for its more grounded approach to the material, despite its occasional flights of fancy.
